source_publication_aliases_unchanged.attests_basis:
The book names no Latin exemplar on any page opened for this lane. Its own
edition record in this repository states that the Latin it prints in the left
column is the Missale Romanum as revised through Benedict XV, and the pages read
here bear that out negatively rather than positively: the body carries the
pre-1955 Holy Week, the Assumption still has its octave, and no page read here
cites a typical edition or a decree. So the edge is a date bound and nothing
stronger. The base text is the 1945 revision, which falls after the typical
edition of 1920 and before maxima-redemptionis-1955, and editio-typica-1920 is
the state it can be translating.

What that bound settles is the same thing it settles for the two Cummiskey
printings this file already carries: every English word quoted from this book is
PRE-1955 English. It witnesses nothing about the restored Holy Week, and the
nineteen Holy Week rows in `untranslated` are beyond its reach for that reason
and not for want of looking.

The act history does not carry this witness. `check-calendar-masses` binds a
source row to the act history only where both files hold the same id, so this
row states its edge on its own account. If the act history later takes the book
up, the two must be held to agree, as the Cummiskey rows already are.

ONE THING THE HELD ARTIFACT IS NOT. The scanned printing is of about 1955-56,
not of 1945, and it carries matter added after 1945. Which matter, and what
follows for the entries below, is set out in the lane report under "the lettered
pages". Five readings formerly quoted from pages numbered 1302a to 1302d were
quarantined on 2026-08-26 because those inserted leaves are not within the
rights basis established for this book. Their text-free targets remain in the
untranslated ledger below.

record.rights_basis: Public domain in the United States because the book was first published outside the United States before the pre-1931 line, and on that ground alone. THE LINE, AND THE YEAR IT WAS DERIVED FOR. Any work first published abroad before 1931 is out of United States copyright; that is the line guidance/missals.md records from Cornell's public-domain chart as current on 1 January 2026. THE LINE MOVES EVERY JANUARY, which guidance/missals.md:249 states in terms, so it is written here as derived for calendar year 2026 and not as a standing rule: on 1 January 2027 it becomes before 1932, and a later reader must re-derive it rather than quote this sentence. Publication at Ratisbon in 1862 clears the line by sixty-nine years, so the line would have to advance to 1863 -- not before 2095 at one year a January -- before it reached this book. AND RESTORATION CANNOT REACH IT EITHER. Restoration under 17 U.S.C. 104A grants a foreign work the remainder of the term it would have had, generally ninety-five years from publication; for 1862 that ran out at the close of 1957, so there was nothing left to restore on 1 January 1996, and the Holy See's Berne accession of 12 September 1935 and Bavaria's earlier adherence are alike beside the point. THE SCAN AND ITS TEXT LAYER ADD NOTHING FOR ANYONE TO OWN. A faithful mechanical reproduction of a public-domain work is not original authorship (Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp., 36 F. Supp. 2d 191 (S.D.N.Y. 1999)), and machine optical character recognition adds no human authorship on top of it: the Internet Archive item's own metadata names the recogniser as ABBYY FineReader 9.0 with abbyy-to-hocr 1.1.11 and the page images as Google's -- scanner google, sponsor Google, google-id E7sPAAAAIAAJ, source books.google.com -- and whichever of the two parties ran the recogniser, it was a program and not a person, so there is no author to hold a right in the text layer. AND THE GOOGLE MATTER WAS LOOKED FOR IN THESE BYTES RATHER THAN ASSUMED FROM THE FIRST PAGE; SEE `notes`, WHICH RECORDS THE SEARCHES, WHAT THEY RETURNED, AND WHY NEITHER OF THE TWO ROUTES OFFERED FOR IT WAS TAKEN. THE BOOK'S OWN PRINTING PRIVILEGES ARE NOT A LIVE RIGHT EITHER. It reprints Clement VIII's and Urban VIII's prohibitions on unlicensed printing of the Missal and carries the Bishop of Ratisbon's licence to Pustet of 1 September 1861; those are ecclesiastical printing controls of the sixteenth to nineteenth centuries, they were never United States copyright, and no party to them claims anything now. THE GOOGLE QUESTION, DECIDED ON THE BYTES. This is a Google digitisation -- its fifth line OCRs as 'Digitized by Googl' and the stamp stands whole at line 79 -- which is why the fold-in of this book was held back from the three that went first. Two routes were offered: land a derivative with the Google matter removed by one stated replayable transformation, or register the scan remote and unresolved and hold no bytes. NEITHER WAS TAKEN, and the reason is a fact about this file.

  WHAT IS NOT HERE. Google's front-matter statement -- 'This is a digital copy of a book that was preserved for generations on library shelves', the 'Usage guidelines', 'About Google Book Search' -- is ABSENT. Searched case-insensitively over the whole 2,503,914 bytes: 'usage guidelines' 0, 'about this book' 0, 'books.google' 0, 'do not assume' 0, 'watermark' 0, 'non-commercial' 0, 'attribution' 0, 'creative commons' 0, 'all rights' 0, 'public domain' 0, and 'copyright' 0. Not one word of Google-authored prose is in this file, and no notice, licence, reservation or condition of any kind appears in it.

  WHAT IS HERE. The page-foot stamp alone: 546 lines contain the string 'google', and a wider sweep that also catches the mangled forms finds about 904 lines in 238 distinct spellings -- 'Digitized by Google' 470 times, then a bare 'Digitized by' 119 times where the word was cut off, 'Digitized by Googl', 'Digitized by GooqIc', 'Digitized by Goegle', 'kJ by Google', and two hundred more. Four words at the foot of a page. It states who ran the scanner, grants nothing and reserves nothing.

  WHY NOT ROUTE (a), THE DERIVATIVE. Because no single stated transformation removes the stamp, and the file is the proof. A strict pattern on 'Digitized by Google' leaves more than four hundred mangled forms behind, which would misrepresent the derivative as clean. A pattern loose enough to catch 'jitized by Google' and 'd by Google' also matches running Latin: the Ritus servandus and De defectibus are full of 'digiti', 'digitis' and 'digitorum' -- at lines 8751, 8968, 8972, 8975, 9085, 9285 and 9664, among others -- and deleting those lines would cut rubrics about the celebrant's fingers out of a Missal. The honest choices were a stated rule with a known large residue or an unstated hand-picked list, and the second is exactly what the offered route forbids.

  WHY NOT ROUTE (b), REMOTE AND UNRESOLVED. Because 'unresolved' would record a doubt these bytes disprove. The doubt was that a public-domain text had Google's own matter added to it; the search above shows it has not, beyond a four-word stamp with no claim in it.

  AND THE DISTINCTION IS CHECKABLE, NOT CONVENIENT. This repository already holds the contrasting case. `artifact.eugene-cummiskey.roman-missal-english-laity.philadelphia-1843.ia-djvu-ocr`, Internet Archive item romanmissaltran00englgoog, stands remote and unresolved for precisely this reason and earns it: its lines 1 to 65 are Google's front-matter block entire, 'Usage guidelines' at line 16 and 'About Google Book Search' at line 60 [verified 2026-08-01 on a fetched copy]. That item has the block and no page stamp; this one has the stamp and no block. Same test, opposite findings.

  THE STAMP IS RETAINED, deliberately. It carries no notice and no claim, so removing it buys nothing; it is the only page-boundary evidence in this text layer; and the Lasance fold-in already set the precedent by retaining the 'http://ccwatershed.org' stamp at the foot of every page of its scan. A reader must not mistake it for a rights notice, and must expect it interleaved through any quotation that spans a page break.

OCR QUALITY, AND IT IS THE BEST OF THE FIVE LATIN AND ENGLISH SCANS FOLDED IN FROM THIS CORPUS. Measured here by scripts/_ocr_quality.py at a Latin function-word share of 0.1792 over 357,261 tokens, English 0.033, classified `prose-latin` -- comfortably above the roughly ten per cent at which that tool says running Latin prose sits, and more than twice the 1570's and the 1604's. The reason is the type: this is a clean nineteenth-century roman face on machine paper, not sixteenth-century abbreviated printing. Whole paragraphs of the bulls, the rubrics and the Canon read straight through. The damage that remains is characteristic and not random: the printed accents on the Latin OCR as digits and punctuation ('mis6ric6rdiam', 'D6minum', 'devoti6ne'), so a search for an accented word will fail where the same word unaccented succeeds; running heads fuse to body text; and the tables, the calendar and the errata list -- which are set in small type and columns -- are wreckage. record.title: Missale Romanum, the Pustet printing of Ratisbon, 1862: a commercial hand-format printing conformed to the Roman text, NOT a typical edition
record.publication: The title page reads MISSALE ROMANUM EX DECRETO SACROSANCTI CONCILII TRIDENTINI RESTITUTUM, S. PII V. PONTIFICIS MAXIMI JUSSU EDITUM, CLEMENTIS VIII. ET URBANI VIII. AUCTORITATE RECOGNITUM, then ACCURATISSIMA EDITIO CUM ADDITAMENTIS NOVISSIMIS, CUM APPROBATIONE SACRORUM RITUUM CONGREGATIONIS, and beneath that RATISBONAE, MDCCCLXII, SUMTIBUS CHARTIS ET TYPIS FRIDERICI PUSTET. The colophon after the appendix reads Ratisbonae: Ex Officina Fr. Pustet, S. Sedis Apostolicae Typographi. Internet Archive item bub_gb_E7sPAAAAIAAJ, a Google digitisation of the New York Public Library's copy; LCCN 33036844, OCLC 7426908.
record.authority: NO PROMULGATING AUTHORITY OF ITS OWN. The authority this book carries is an approbation, not a promulgation, and the difference is the whole of why this record exists. Ignatius von Senestrey, Bishop of Ratisbon, subscribed letters at Ratisbon on 1 September 1861, printed in the book at lines 712 to 745 of the text layer, which recite that by the decrees of Clement VIII, Urban VIII and others no printer may publish the Roman Missal unless the conformity of the new edition with the Roman archetypes is plainly established and the licence to print it has been sought and obtained from the Ordinary of the place; that two priests were deputed at Frederick Pustet's petition to examine this hand-format edition; that they reported it conformed to the authentic Roman exemplars and that the additions and corrections prescribed by the Sacred Congregation of Rites on 26 September 1860 and by Pius IX on 27 September 1860 and 12 March 1861 had been inserted or noted; and that the bishop therefore approves it and grants licence to publish. That is a licence to print a book, granted by a local ordinary to a commercial firm. It is not an act of the Holy See imposing a text.
record.notes:
THIS IS A PRINTING AND NOT A TYPICAL EDITION, AND NOTHING MAY BE INFERRED FROM ITS DATE ABOUT THE HISTORY OF THE RITE. The audit that authorised this fold-in required the point be recorded in terms and named the specific harm: src/sources/inventories/missal-acquisition-audit-v1.toml records that a generator once chained books by date and thereby asserted that a rite descends through a publisher, and 'the 1862 Pustet printing' is one of the two books it was caught on. The schema has no `is_typical_edition` field to carry the denial, so it is carried here, in prose, at the top of the record where a reader meets it before the date.

THE BOOK SAYS SO ITSELF, TWICE, IN ITS OWN WORDS. Its title page claims only to be an ACCURATISSIMA EDITIO CUM ADDITAMENTIS NOVISSIMIS printed at Pustet's expense and types. Its approbation, quoted under `authority`, is a bishop's licence granted because a printer proved conformity with the Roman archetypes -- the argument of a copy, not of an original. And its publisher's note to the reader, headed Typographus Ratisbonensis Lectori at line 101601, states what was copied: 'Hic finem habet Romana, anno 1856 typis Josephi Salviucci et Francisci filii perfecta editio, quam nostris Ratisbonensibus typis minori hac ac manuali forma reproducendam curavimus' -- here ends the Roman edition completed in 1856 by the press of Giuseppe Salviucci and son, which we have had reproduced in our Ratisbon types in this smaller and hand-sized format. So the text descends from a Rome 1856 printing, itself a printing of the Clement VIII and Urban VIII recension, and this book is a reduced-format reproduction of it. The line of descent is Pius V 1570, Clement VIII 1604, Urban VIII 1634; Salviucci 1856 and Pustet 1862 stand outside it.

WHAT PUSTET ADDED IS ALSO THE PUBLISHER'S AND NOT THE RITE'S. The same note explains the appendix: because many wanted at hand the Masses granted to particular provinces or dioceses which the Roman edition does not contain, the firm gathered the commoner of them out of diocesan and religious Propria printed with their own ordinaries' authority and collected them under the name of an Appendix. Those Masses, and the Calendarium festorum pro aliquibus locis concessorum that follows the colophon, are a publisher's compilation of indults. The front matter likewise carries a stack of Sacred Congregation of Rites decrees of 1861 and 1862 obtained for particular petitioners -- the Japanese Martyrs' Mass at Propaganda Fide's request on 10 July 1862, Blessed John Leonardi for his congregation and the diocese of Lucca on 5 June 1862, a monitum on St Angela Merici of 11 July 1861 -- each of which grants a Mass to somebody, and none of which promulgates a Missal. The publisher's own errata list, headed Emendanda juxta S. Rit. Congregationis decretum de die 25. Sept. 1860, admits that not every sheet was corrected before the decrees were published, so this printing is not even internally uniform.

WHAT THE COPY CARRIES. Quo primum from line 152, the Sacred Congregation decrees and the Ratisbon approbation in the front matter, the Rubricae generales Missalis from line 8001, the Ritus servandus in celebratione Missarum from line 8674, De defectibus in its numbered divisions from line 11015, the temporal and sanctoral Masses, and the Canon entire under the running head CANON MISSAE at line 41068, with Qui pridie quam pateretur at line 41219. The Latin carries printed accents throughout, which the 1570 and 1604 scans in this library do not.

IT IS THE ALTAR BOOK AND NOT A HAND MISSAL, notwithstanding its 'hand-sized format', which means a small altar Missal and not a lay book: it is entirely in Latin, it prints the rubrics for the celebrant, and it has no lay devotions. The English lay missals registered in this library are a different genre and are not witnesses to this or any other Latin edition's text.
